\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Gujarati, recognize the reply, choose an appropriate response, and write \gu{હા} from a heard cue after learning its two pieces.}

Complete GU-C01-practice, greet someone in Gujarati, choose an appropriate response, and retrieve \gu{હા} in writing from sound with no visible model.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[namaste]{Namaste — first hear the greeting}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-namaste}



\begin{quote}
Imagine meeting someone at the start of the day. First, only listen: \emph{namaste}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\emph{Namaste} works as a greeting when you meet someone. You can also hear it at a leave-taking. For this first pass, the sound and social job are enough: hear \emph{na-ma-ste}, then answer with the same greeting.

The Gujarati spelling is deliberately not decoded here. The next ten tiny lessons will give your eye and hand one reusable piece at a time. Only after all six pieces of this word are familiar will the book ask you to read or copy it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Namaste} continues Sanskrit \emph{namas}, \textquotedblleft{}a bow,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{te}, \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}: literally, \textquotedblleft{}a bow to you.\textquotedblright{} Gujarati inherited the greeting through its Indo-Aryan history. You do not need to remember the two historical pieces yet; they are simply a memory hook for the greeting's respectful shape.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}namaste\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}namaste\textquotedblright{} once as a greeting and once as a leave-taking
  \item its literal memory hook (\textquotedblleft{}a bow to you\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What can you say when you meet someone? (\emph{\textbf{Namaste.}}) What is its literal memory hook? (\emph{\textbf{A bow to you.}}) Do you need to read its Gujarati spelling yet? (\textbf{No} — the script ramp starts next, one piece at a time.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ha]{\gu{હ} — the consonant ha}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-ha}



\begin{quote}
Say the greeting from the previous lesson once. Now let speech rest: today your hand meets only one reusable Gujarati consonant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Gujarati is written with an \textbf{abugida}, and that word is doing a lot of work. It is not an alphabet, where each letter is one sound. It is a system where \textbf{a consonant already carries a vowel}, and you only write a vowel when you want a different one.

Here is the first consonant:

\begin{quote}
\gu{હ}
\end{quote}

That is not \emph{h}. It is \textbf{ha} — the consonant \emph{h} with an \textbf{a} already inside it, the \emph{a} of English \emph{about}. Nobody wrote that vowel. It is there because a bare consonant in this script is understood to carry it, and this is called the \textbf{inherent vowel}.

Look at the shape while you say it. Notice what is \textbf{not} there: no line across the top. Gujarati is Devanagari's sister and the two share most of their skeleton, but Devanagari hangs its letters from a horizontal bar and Gujarati has erased it. The letters float. That single missing line is how you tell the two scripts apart at a glance, and it is why Gujarati is sometimes called \textbf{the headless script}.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace one consonant}
Keep \textbf{\gu{હ}} visible. Finger-trace it once, slowly, then trace it once in the air. Say \emph{ha} after your finger stops. Do not try to write the word for \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} yet; its vowel sign comes next.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel does a bare consonant carry? (\textbf{a} — the inherent vowel, unwritten.) And what is the one visible difference from Devanagari? (\textbf{No line across the top}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ā]{\gu{ા} — the vowel sign that replaces the inherent a}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-aa-matra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
The inherent \textbf{a} is a default. To get a different vowel you \textbf{replace} it, and you replace it with a mark called a \textbf{mātrā}.

Here is the first one:

\begin{quote}
\gu{ા}
\end{quote}

On its own it is nothing — a vertical stroke you would never write alone. It only means anything \textbf{attached to a consonant}, where it swaps the inherent short \emph{a} for a long \textbf{ā}, the \emph{a} of English \emph{father}.

Place it immediately to the right of the consonant you just learned:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{હ}} + \textbf{\gu{ા}}
\end{quote}

Together they sound \textbf{hā}. Keep the pieces separated on this first pass so your hand learns the sign itself rather than copying a whole-word picture. A later spoken lesson will give that sound a conversational job.

Take the measure of that. You learned one consonant and one mark, and they made a syllable you can \textbf{read}. Nothing was memorised as a picture.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace one vowel sign}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ા}} visible beside \textbf{\gu{હ}}. Finger-trace the vowel sign once, then point to where it attaches on the consonant. Say \emph{hā}. You are not copying a whole word yet; today is only the second piece.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a mātrā do to the inherent vowel? (\textbf{Replaces} it.) What syllable do those two separate pieces make together? (\emph{\textbf{Hā.}})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\gu{આ} — the SAME vowel standing alone}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-aa}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Now a distinction that trips up every beginner in every Indic script, and it is worth meeting deliberately rather than by accident.

The mark you just learned only works \textbf{attached to a consonant}. So what do you write when a word \textbf{starts} with that vowel, with no consonant to hang it on?

You write a different character:

\begin{quote}
\gu{આ}
\end{quote}

That is \textbf{ā} as well — the same sound — but it is an \textbf{independent vowel}, a full letter that stands on its own at the start of a word.

\textbf{These are two different characters, not two styles of one.} They look related because they are, and a computer, a font and this book all treat them as completely separate. Confusing them is the commonest spelling error in the script.

So what decides which one you write is \textbf{position}, not sound:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{આ}} begins a word.
  \item \textbf{\gu{ા}} rides on a consonant.
\end{itemize}

You already know a word that opens with the independent one — the word for \emph{thanks} — and you will be able to read the whole of it shortly.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{આ} visible and trace it once with a finger
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two starts a word? (\textbf{\gu{આ}}, the independent vowel.) Which one attaches to a consonant? (\textbf{\gu{ા}}, the mātrā.) And are they the same character? (\textbf{No} — two separate characters for one sound.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\gu{ન} — the consonant na}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-na}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\gu{ન}
\end{quote}

\textbf{na}, with the same inherent \textbf{a} inside it. The \emph{n} of English \emph{net}, then the vowel nobody wrote.

This is also the first written piece of the greeting you already know by ear. Keep the whole greeting hidden for now. One consonant is enough work for one tiny lesson.

If you later attach the long-aa sign, the sound becomes \emph{nā}. That is the arithmetic of an abugida: consonants and vowel signs multiply, so a small number of pieces reaches a large number of syllables. Today you only trace bare \textbf{\gu{ન}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{ન} visible and trace it once with a finger

\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the bare consonant sound like on its own? (\emph{\textbf{Na}}, with the inherent vowel.) What happens if a vowel sign is attached later? (It \textbf{replaces} that inherent vowel.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.

\section[ma]{\gu{મ} — the consonant ma}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-ma}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\gu{મ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ma}. The \emph{m} of English \emph{met}, with the inherent \textbf{a} riding along.

Nothing new in the machinery this time — this is simply another consonant, and the rules you already have apply to it unchanged. Add the mātrā and you would get \emph{mā}; leave it bare and it is \emph{ma}.

That is worth saying plainly, because it is the payoff of learning the system rather than the words. \textbf{Every consonant from here behaves exactly like the two you already know.} There are no new rules coming for them, only new shapes.

Write it beside the two you have. Three letters, floating, no bar across the top.

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{મ} visible and trace it once with a finger
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel is inside \textbf{\gu{મ}} when nothing is attached? (\textbf{a}.) And what would \textbf{\gu{મ}} plus the mātrā you know sound like? (\emph{\textbf{mā}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sa]{\gu{સ} — the consonant sa}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-sa}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\gu{સ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{sa}. The \emph{s} of English \emph{sit}, plus the inherent vowel.

You are four consonants and one mātrā into this script, and every one of them has behaved the same way. Say the four aloud in the order you met them, each with its inherent vowel:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{હ}}   \textbf{\gu{ન}}   \textbf{\gu{મ}}   \textbf{\gu{સ}}
\end{quote}

\emph{ha, na, ma, sa.} Four beats, four shapes, no bar across any of them.

\section[ta]{\gu{ત} — the consonant ta}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-ta}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\gu{ત}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ta} — and the consonant is not quite the English one.

English \emph{t} is made with the tongue on the \textbf{ridge behind} the teeth. This one is \textbf{dental}: the tongue touches the \textbf{back of the upper teeth themselves}, further forward. It sounds softer to an English ear, and getting it right is one of the quickest ways to stop sounding foreign.

The script will make you care about this shortly, because it has a \textbf{second} t made even further back, and the two are different letters and different words. This is the forward one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{ત} visible and trace it once with a finger
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the tongue go for \textbf{\gu{ત}}? (Against the \textbf{back of the upper teeth} — dental, not on the ridge.) And is there another t in this script? (\textbf{Yes}, one made further back.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-e]{\gu{ે} — a mātrā that sits ABOVE the letter, not beside it}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-e-matra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
A second vowel sign, and it introduces something the first one did not.

\begin{quote}
\gu{ે}
\end{quote}

This is \textbf{e}, the vowel of English \emph{bed}. And unlike the mātrā you already know, which stands to the \textbf{right} of its consonant, this one sits \textbf{above} it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ત}} + \textbf{\gu{ે}} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{તે}}
\end{quote}

\emph{te.} One beat, still — the mark changes the vowel, never the count.

\textbf{Where a mātrā sits is not decoration.} In this family of scripts a vowel sign can go to the right, to the left, above, below, or even on both sides at once, and the position is part of the character's identity. A reader learns to look \textbf{around} a consonant, not just after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{ે} visible and trace it once with a finger
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does this mātrā sit? (\textbf{Above} the consonant.) Does it add a beat? (\textbf{No} — it replaces the vowel, it does not add one.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(virama)]{\gu{્} — the mark that DELETES the inherent vowel, and glues two consonants together}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-virama}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
One piece of machinery left, and it is the one that makes the script's hardest shapes make sense.

The inherent vowel is a nuisance when you do not want it. If a word has two consonants pressed together with no vowel between them, writing them plainly would insert an \emph{a} that is not there.

So there is a mark that \textbf{removes} it:

\begin{quote}
\gu{્}
\end{quote}

This is the \textbf{virama}. Attached under a consonant, it says: \emph{no vowel here.}

And then something happens that no European alphabet does. A consonant stripped of its vowel does not usually sit there bare — it \textbf{fuses} with the consonant after it into a single joined shape called a \textbf{conjunct}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{સ}} + \textbf{\gu{્}} + \textbf{\gu{ત}} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{સ્ત}}
\end{quote}

\emph{sta}, one cluster. You can still see both letters in it if you look, and that is the trick to reading conjuncts: they are not new characters to memorise, they are two you already know, joined.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} keep \gu{્} visible and trace it once with a finger
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the virama do? (\textbf{Removes the inherent vowel}.) And what usually happens to a consonant that loses its vowel? (It \textbf{joins} the next one into a conjunct.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[namaste]{\gu{નમસ્તે} — five pieces, all of them already yours}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-namaste-read}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Everything in this word is something you can already write. Nothing new is introduced here at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ન}} + \textbf{\gu{મ}} + \textbf{\gu{સ}} + \textbf{\gu{્}} + \textbf{\gu{ત}} + \textbf{\gu{ે}} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{નમસ્તે}}
\end{quote}

Read it the way you built it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{ન}} — \emph{na}, inherent vowel
  \item \textbf{\gu{મ}} — \emph{ma}, inherent vowel
  \item \textbf{\gu{સ્ત}} — the conjunct: \emph{sa} with its vowel removed, fused to \emph{ta}
  \item \textbf{\gu{ે}} — the mātrā above, making that last piece \emph{te}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{na-ma-ste.} The greeting you learned in your first lesson, now decoded rather than recalled.

The greeting itself takes \textbf{four consonants, one vowel sign, and one virama}. The extra consonant and long-vowel pieces you traced on the way will pay off in the next few spoken words. Every consonant you meet from here follows the same inherent-vowel rule, so the next word costs new shapes but not a new system.

The script has around forty more letters. It does not have any more \textbf{systems}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Copy:} keep \gu{નમસ્તે} visible and copy it once, piece by piece
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new pieces were in this lesson? (\textbf{None}.) What is \textbf{\gu{સ્ત}} made of? (\emph{\textbf{\gu{સ}}} with its vowel removed, joined to \emph{\textbf{\gu{ત}}}.) And what does the mark above the last letter do? (Makes it \emph{\textbf{te}} instead of \emph{ta}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આભાર}]{\gu{આભાર} (ābhār) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} an obligation gladly owed}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aabhaar}



\begin{quote}
Gujarati's everyday \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} — and it comes from the idea of being \emph{indebted}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (the independent long \emph{ā}, for a word-initial vowel) + \textbf{\gu{ભા}} (\emph{bhā}) + \textbf{\gu{ર}} (\emph{r}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}). Note again: no top line.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}, \textquotedblleft{}thanks, gratitude\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhāra}, \textquotedblleft{}a burden, an obligation\textquotedblright{}), from \textbf{\gu{આ}-} (\emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) + the root \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}} (\emph{bhṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to bear, carry\textquotedblright{}). To thank someone is to acknowledge you now \emph{bear an obligation} to them — the same idea as English \textbf{oblige} (Latin \emph{ob-} + \emph{ligāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}) and Portuguese \emph{obrigado}. That root \emph{bhṛ} is Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, the ancestor of English \textbf{bear} (to carry) and Latin \emph{ferre}. (The more Sanskritic \textbf{\gu{ધન્યવાદ}} \emph{dhanyavād} is also used, but \emph{ābhār} is the warm, everyday Gujarati word.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ābhār\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally acknowledges (an obligation \textquotedblleft{}borne\textquotedblright{})
  \item the English cousin of its root \emph{bhṛ} (\textbf{bear}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ābhār} literally mean, and what English word shares its root? (\textquotedblleft{}An obligation borne\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{bear} — from PIE \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આવજો}]{\gu{આવજો} (āvjo) — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{} (come again)}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aavjo}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Gujarati goodbye — and, like the goodbyes across all of India, it is really an invitation to return.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (independent \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\gu{વ}} (\emph{va}) + \textbf{\gu{જો}} (\emph{jo}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}) is the polite imperative of \textbf{\gu{આવવું}} (\emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}}.\textquotedblright{} A Gujarati never signs off by saying \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{}; the parting word is \emph{come}. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} that runs through the whole subcontinent — Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}), Bengali \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come\textquotedblright{}), Hindi \emph{phir milenge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}) — here made into a single warm word built on the verb \emph{to come}. (To one person, familiarly: \textbf{\gu{આવજે}} \emph{āvje}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āvjo\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{})
  \item the verb it's built on (\emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Gujarati goodbye literally say, and what verb is it from? (\textquotedblleft{}Come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{} — never \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{હા} / \gu{ના}]{\gu{હા} / \gu{ના} (hā / nā) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-haa-naa}



\begin{quote}
Two tiny words no conversation survives without — and one is a cousin of English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}) = \textbf{\gu{હ}} (\emph{ha}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign. \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}) = \textbf{\gu{ન}} (\emph{na}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}). The \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} rides the ancient negative \textbf{na-} — the very same Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}, Latin \emph{nōn}, Hindi \emph{nahīṁ}, and Bengali \emph{nā}. Of all the words in this book, this \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} reaches furthest unchanged: one syllable spoken, in some form, from Iceland to Gujarat for five thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hā\textquotedblright{} (yes) and \textquotedblleft{}nā\textquotedblright{} (no)
  \item the shared ancestor of \emph{nā} and English \emph{no} (PIE \emph{*ne})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ancient root links Gujarati \emph{nā} to English \emph{no}? (Proto-Indo- European \emph{*ne}, \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{\gu{હા} — one supported copy}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to the consonant \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then the attached vowel sign \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Say the whole known word: \textbf{\gu{હા}}, \emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{} Keep the model visible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\gu{હા}} once. You may look back after each piece: first \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Touch both pieces in your copy and read \emph{hā}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare only the two pieces and their order. Repair one piece if needed, then stop. The model stays visible today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{\gu{હા} — look, hide, write, compare}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Look at \textbf{\gu{હા}} for five seconds. Point first to \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then to \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Do not copy it yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
1. cover \textbf{\gu{હા}} 2. wait five seconds 3. write it once from memory 4. uncover the model and compare the two pieces

If one piece differs, circle it and repair only that place. Repair is part of the exercise, not a failure.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read your repaired word as \emph{hā}. Stop after one memory attempt.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{One heard answer — write what you know}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover the answer lower on this page. You will hear one familiar answer. No new Gujarati is hiding in this lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — short dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{hā} — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}{]}

Write the Gujarati word from sound alone. Now uncover and compare: \textbf{\gu{હા}}. Check \textbf{\gu{હ}} first and attached \textbf{\gu{ા}} second. Repair one place if needed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Writing from sound completes this tiny runway. It is not a mock assessment; later lessons must grow from one known word to forms, messages, and timed tasks.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{સારું}]{\gu{સારું} (sārũ) — \textquotedblleft{}good,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-saarun}



\begin{quote}
The all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}good / fine / okay / alright\textquotedblright{} — and your first taste of Gujarati's three genders.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{સા}} (\emph{sā}) + \textbf{\gu{રું}} (\emph{rũ}, with the nasal \emph{anusvāra} on the \emph{u}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}good, fine, okay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{સાર}} (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence, substance, the best part\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{sāra} behind Bengali's \emph{sāramilla} (\textquotedblleft{}no matter\textquotedblright{}). As \textquotedblleft{}okay/agreed\textquotedblright{} it oils every Gujarati conversation, the way English uses \textquotedblleft{}alright.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three genders, on the adjective}]
Look at that ending \textbf{-\gu{ું}} (\emph{-ũ}). Gujarati, like Marathi, keeps \textbf{three} genders from Sanskrit — masculine, feminine, \textbf{and neuter} — where Hindi and Punjabi kept only two. An adjective agrees with its noun in all three:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારો}} (\emph{sāro}) — masculine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારી}} (\emph{sārī}) — feminine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}) — \textbf{neuter}
\end{itemize}

Standing alone as \textquotedblleft{}okay,\textquotedblright{} it takes the neuter \emph{sārũ}. You will meet this three-way agreement on every adjective and possessive.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sārũ\textquotedblright{} — good / okay
  \item the three genders — \emph{sāro} (m.) / \emph{sārī} (f.) / \emph{sārũ} (n.)
  \item the Sanskrit root (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sārũ} mean, and what does its \emph{-ũ} ending tell you? (\textquotedblleft{}Good / okay\textquotedblright{}; it is the \textbf{neuter} — Gujarati keeps three genders.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — The greetings}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The five greetings, mixed and recombined.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — rapid recall}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hello / goodbye — \emph{namaste}
  \item thank you — \emph{ābhār}
  \item yes and no — \emph{hā} / \emph{nā}
  \item good / okay — \emph{sārũ}
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{} goodbye — \emph{āvjo}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the script and the language}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the one visible thing that sets Gujarati apart from Devanagari (no top line)
  \item how many genders Gujarati keeps (three — \emph{sāro/sārī/sārũ})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing — retrieve the tiny word once}
Cover every written answer. Hear \emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes,\textquotedblright{} once in your mind and write it from memory. Then uncover \textbf{\gu{હા}} and check the two pieces: \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then attached \textbf{\gu{ા}}. One repair is allowed.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaste} = \emph{namas} \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{te} \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{ābhār} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ā} + \emph{bhṛ} \textquotedblleft{}to bear\textquotedblright{} $\to$ an obligation borne (cousin of English \emph{bear})
  \item \emph{nā} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne} $\to$ English \emph{no/not/none}
  \item \emph{āvjo} (\textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}come {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} from \emph{āvvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Someone thanks you and turns to leave. Answer their thanks and send them off the Gujarati way. (\emph{Sārũ} — and \emph{āvjo}, \textquotedblleft{}come again.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
